subject: Sedaghatian (1980)
object: Sedaghatian (1980) reported 2 brothers, born within a year of each other, with a similar skeletal disorder. It consisted of severe congenital metaphyseal involvement, mild rhizomelic shortness of the upper limbs, and mild platyspondyly. Both died at 3 days of age of cardiorespiratory insufficiency.

subject: Sedaghatian (1980)
object: Sedaghatian (1980) found that only one of the 2 affected brothers had laboratory tests before death. These showed low calcium, high phosphorus, and high alkaline phosphatase levels, which were attributed to a renal defect.

subject: Sedaghatian (1980)
object: Sedaghatian (1980) reported that autopsy of the same infant showed pulmonary, renal, and adrenal hemorrhage, along with subendocardial myocarditis and myocardial necrosis. The author stated that the pathogenetic relationship between these manifestations was unclear.

subject: Sedaghatian (1980)
object: The parents of the affected brothers reported by Sedaghatian (1980) were normal and had recently had an affected baby girl. On this basis the author presumed autosomal recessive inheritance.

subject: Opitz et al. (1987)
object: Opitz et al. (1987) reported another Iranian infant with Sedaghatian syndrome who died on day 4 of life. Histology showed severe epimetaphyseal dysplasia.

subject: Opitz et al. (1987)
object: Opitz et al. (1987) summarized Sedaghatian's 1980 report of 2 brothers and a sister with a neonatally lethal disorder marked by slight rhizomelic limb shortening, mild platyspondyly, and severe metaphyseal dysplasia. They suggested the syndrome may be more complexly pleiotropic than the radiographs indicate, because one of Sedaghatian's patients also had microphthalmia, asymmetric ears, depressed nasal bridge, broad nose, short neck, prominent sternum, and short lower extremities.

subject: Opitz et al. (1987)
object: Opitz et al. (1987) suggested that Sedaghatian syndrome is an autosomal recessive trait with a high gene frequency in Iranians. Their reasons were that children of both sexes were affected in one family, the parents were normal first cousins, and the disorder had so far been seen only in Iranians.

subject: Peeden et al. (1992)
object: Peeden et al. (1992) reported another infant with spondylometaphyseal dysplasia, Sedaghatian type, who had a lethal course.

subject: Peeden et al. (1992)
object: Peeden et al. (1992) reviewed the Iranian infant described by Sedaghatian in 1980, who died shortly after birth. At autopsy he had subacute myocarditis, cortical necrosis of the kidneys, and adrenal and pulmonary hemorrhage. His skeletal findings were mild rhizomelic shortening of the limbs, platyspondyly, and 'laciness' of the iliac wings.

subject: Peeden et al. (1992)
object: Peeden et al. (1992) noted that the second reported Iranian infant, described by Opitz et al. in 1987, had a similar perinatal course and similar radiographs. Because this infant was born to first-cousin parents, the authors suggested autosomal recessive inheritance of a single-gene defect.

subject: Elçioglu and Hall (1998)
object: Elçioglu and Hall (1998) reported the radiological findings in 2 unrelated cases of spondylometaphyseal dysplasia, Sedaghatian type. After reviewing the literature, they identified additional anomalies, including disproportionately long fibulae, dysharmonious maturation, and turricephaly.

subject: Koutouby et al. (2000)
object: Koutouby et al. (2000) reported an infant with spondylometaphyseal dysplasia born to nonconsanguineous Yemeni parents. The radiologic findings were consistent with lethal metaphyseal chondrodysplasia, Sedaghatian type. All previously reported patients had died within 4 days of life, but this patient survived 161 days.

subject: Koutouby et al. (2000)
object: Koutouby et al. (2000) investigated the patient with serum calcium, magnesium, zinc, ammonia, phosphate, alkaline phosphatase and parathormone levels, liver and renal function tests, TORCH, metabolic screening, chromosomal studies, muscle enzymes, EEG, CT scan and brain MRI. Genomic DNA from the patient and parents was analyzed, but no gene abnormality was found.

subject: English et al. (2006)
object: English et al. (2006) reported a female infant with Sedaghatian spondylometaphyseal dysplasia. She was born to nonconsanguineous Caucasian parents and had a metaphyseal dysplasia. She was hypotonic from birth and had recurrent cyanotic episodes within a few hours of delivery. Brain imaging showed absence of the corpus callosum and marked frontotemporal pachygyria. She developed seizures on day 14 and died at age 17 days.

subject: English et al. (2006)
object: English et al. (2006) concluded that their case showed neuronal migration abnormalities can occur in Sedaghatian spondylometaphyseal dysplasia. They suggested agenesis of the corpus callosum as a new association of the disorder.

subject: Aygun et al. (2012)
object: Aygun et al. (2012) reported a patient with Sedaghatian-type spondylometaphyseal dysplasia. The patient had metaphyseal dysplasia, congenital atrioventricular block, a simplified gyral pattern, hypogenesis of the corpus callosum, and severe cerebellar hypoplasia. The authors suggested that central nervous system malformations might be a major component of this congenital lethal skeletal dysplasia and should be evaluated in detail.

subject: Smith et al. (2014)
object: Smith et al. (2014) described Sedaghatian-type spondylometaphyseal dysplasia (SSMD) as a neonatal lethal form of spondylometaphyseal dysplasia characterized by severe metaphyseal chondrodysplasia with mild limb shortening, platyspondyly, cardiac conduction defects, and central nervous system abnormalities.

subject: Smith et al. (2014)
object: By whole exome sequencing of a girl with SSMD and her unaffected parents, Smith et al. (2014) identified compound heterozygous variants in GPX4 (NM_001039848.1): a maternally inherited c.587+5G>A splice variant, which in vitro studies showed caused splicing out of part of exon 4, resulting in frameshift and premature truncation.

subject: Smith et al. (2014)
object: In the same girl with SSMD, Smith et al. (2014) identified a de novo GPX4 variant, c.588-8_588-4del (NM_001039848.1), in trans with the maternally inherited c.587+5G>A; in vitro studies showed that it caused skipping of exon 5, resulting in frameshift and premature truncation of GPX4.

subject: Smith et al. (2014)
object: In a second, unrelated child with SSMD whose DNA was not available, Smith et al. (2014) found by Sanger sequencing that both unaffected parents carried the same heterozygous nonsense mutation in exon 3 of GPX4, c.381C>A (p.Tyr127*) (NM_001039848.1).

subject: Smith et al. (2014)
object: Smith et al. (2014) concluded that truncating GPX4 mutations in 2 families with SSMD supported a pathogenic role for GPX4, an antioxidant enzyme that protects cells against membrane lipid peroxidation and is essential for early embryo development. They suggested that their findings highlighted the importance of GPX4 in development of the cardiac, nervous, and skeletal systems.
